subject: Toronto listings fell faster than sales in September
bodyMarkdown:
If you are buying or selling anywhere around Toronto, the September numbers that landed yesterday say both sides of this market have gone quiet at once. That is a different problem from falling prices, and it changes what you should do between now and the spring.

## What the September numbers actually say

The Toronto Regional Real Estate Board reported on Tuesday that GTA agents sold 5,040 homes through the MLS system in September, down 9 per cent from a year earlier. New listings came in at 16,500, down 14.4 per cent. The average selling price was $1,006,409, down 5.1 per cent, and the **MLS Home Price Index** composite benchmark, which strips out the effect of which homes happened to sell that month, was down 4.7 per cent.

Read those together and something odd falls out. Listings dropped faster than sales did. Supply shrinking faster than demand is normally what stops prices from sliding. Prices slid anyway. Nobody is being forced to sell at a discount here. Sellers are pulling their listings and waiting, and the buyers who would have met them are waiting too.

## The condo is where it shows up

The condo apartment told the clearest version of this. The average condo sold for $605,257 in September, down 7.7 per cent over the year, the steepest drop of the four main housing types, while the detached average sat at $1,292,016. Storeys reported that of the 1,316 condos sold across the GTA that month, 893 went for less than $600,000. Call it two in three.

I keep coming back to who is on the other side of those sales. A condo is the entry unit for a first-time buyer and the standard product for a small investor, and a lot of the towers finishing now were sold on paper in 2021 and 2022 at prices this resale market will not pay. A listing can be withdrawn. A closing cannot. That is the supply which has to clear no matter what the benchmark does.

## Why the Bank of Canada will not rescue this

Anyone waiting for a rate cut to restart the market should read what Carolyn Rogers, the Bank's senior deputy governor, told the Greater Victoria Chamber of Commerce last Thursday. House prices, she said, "are now deeply intertwined with household wealth, the stability of our financial system and the strength of our economy", and aiming interest rates at them "would ask monetary policy to do more than it can reasonably do". BNN Bloomberg's headline that day called the policy rate too blunt for the job, which is fair.

The Bank held at 2.25 per cent on September 2, its seventh hold in a row, and said tariffs and oil prices had raised the upside risks to inflation. The next decision lands October 28 with a Monetary Policy Report attached. I would not build a plan around a cut.

## The takeaway

If you are selling, the competition you actually face is thinner than it was a year ago, because the other sellers left too. If you are shopping for a condo under $600,000, you are in the one corner of this market where the person across the table has a deadline and you do not. Watch the October 28 report for what the Bank says about shelter costs rather than for the rate itself, because the rate is probably staying put. And watch next month's listing count, since sellers returning before buyers do is what turns 4.7 per cent into a bigger number.
